n: Men who had been castrated or emasculated — sometimes as part of pagan temple service — could not join Israel’s formal assembly. Isaiah later promised such faithful people a place in God’s house.

f.g: Israel’s official assembly for worship and decision-making.
Castrated.

n: Someone born of a forbidden union was excluded for many generations. The Hebrew word here is rare and its exact meaning is uncertain.

f.g: Hebrew mamzer — probably a child of incest or a forbidden mixed marriage, not simply one born outside marriage.
An idiom for “permanently.”

n: Ammonites and Moabites were barred from the assembly. Yet Ruth the Moabitess, through faith and conversion, became an ancestor of David and of Jesus.
The reason: they refused hospitality to Israel on the journey and even hired the seer Balaam to curse them.

f.g: A town near the Euphrates River.

n: God refused to curse Israel and turned Balaam’s words into blessings, simply because he loved them.

f.w: turned the curse into a blessing

n: Israel was not to make treaties seeking Ammon’s or Moab’s welfare — that is, no formal alliances.

f.g: Make a treaty or alliance with them.

n: Edomites were relatives — descendants of Jacob’s brother Esau. Egyptians had once hosted Israel. So these were not to be despised.

f.g: Hate, detest.

n: Their descendants could join the assembly after three generations.

f.g: Grandchildren of the first settlers.

n: An army camp must be morally and ritually clean, because God was present with the troops.

f.w: keep thee from every wicked thing

f.g: Army.

n: A man who had a nighttime emission was temporarily ritually unclean and stayed outside the camp.

f.w: uncleanness that chanceth him by night

n: By evening he washed and could return after sunset. Ritual impurity was not sin but required simple steps of cleansing.

f.g: The new day began at sunset.

n: A designated latrine area had to be set up outside the camp.

f.g: Outside the camp.

n: Each soldier carried a digging tool to bury waste — practical hygiene that protected health.

f.g: A digging tool or small spade.
Relieve yourself.

n: The deeper reason: God walks among his people. A clean camp honored his presence. Latter-day Saints see a similar principle in keeping temples and lives clean.

f.w: the LORD thy God walketh in the midst of thy camp

n: A remarkable law: an escaped slave from another land must not be sent back to his master. Israel was to be a refuge.

f.g: Likely a slave fleeing from a foreign country.

n: He could live freely in any town he chose, and no one was to mistreat him.

f.g: Wherever he pleases.

n: No Israelite, man or woman, was to serve as a cult prostitute, a common feature of Canaanite fertility religion.

f.g: Hebrew qedeshah — a woman associated with pagan shrine prostitution.
Hebrew qadesh — a male shrine prostitute.

n: Earnings from prostitution could never be given as an offering to God. Money gained through sin cannot buy holiness.

f.g: Probably a crude term for a male prostitute’s wages.

n: Israelites must not charge interest to one another on loans of money, food, or anything else. Loans to the needy were acts of mercy, not profit.

f.g: In KJV, any interest on a loan, not just excessive interest.
Food.

n: Interest could be charged to foreign traders doing business, but not to fellow Israelites. Generosity brings God’s blessing.

f.w: Unto a stranger thou mayest lend upon usury
f.g: Here “stranger” means a foreigner (nokri), not a resident alien.

n: A vow to God must be kept promptly. Broken promises to God are sin.

f.w: thou shalt not slack to pay it
f.g: Don’t delay in fulfilling it.

n: No one had to make vows; refraining was no sin. But once made, a vow was binding.

f.g: Choose not to vow.

n: Whatever comes out of your mouth as a promise to God, do it. Integrity in speech matters.

f.w: That which is gone out of thy lips

n: A traveler could eat grapes in a neighbor’s vineyard to satisfy hunger, but not fill a basket to carry away.

f.w: thou shalt not put any in thy vessel
f.g: No harvesting for yourself — only eating on the spot.

n: Likewise, hungry passersby could pick grain by hand but not use a sickle. Jesus’ disciples did exactly this.

f.w: pluck the ears with thine hand

f.g: Unharvested grain still in the field.
